title: Kafka Delivery Semantics: At Most Once to Exactly Once
summary: A dense field guide to how Kafka actually delivers messages — the three delivery guarantees, the producer and consumer knobs that pick between them, idempotent producers, transactions, read_committed isolation, and the failure modes that quietly break each one.

chapters.title: Delivery Semantics: The Three Guarantees
points: Definition: at-most-once = every message delivered zero or one time; loss possible, duplicates impossible
Definition: at-least-once = every message delivered one or more times; loss impossible, duplicates possible
Definition: exactly-once = every message has exactly one observable effect; no loss, no duplicate effect
Guarantees are a property of the whole pipeline (produce + store + consume + side effects), not of a single config flag
Two independent halves: producer-to-broker delivery, and consumer-side processing + offset commit
The pipeline guarantee is the weakest of its links — at-least-once producer plus at-most-once consumer = at-most-once end to end
Core cause of duplicates: retry after an ambiguous outcome (request may have succeeded, ack lost on the wire)
Core cause of loss: acknowledging or committing progress before the data is durable or processed
The retry dilemma: on timeout you must either retry (risk duplicate) or not (risk loss) — you cannot avoid both without deduplication
Kafka's exactly-once is 'exactly-once processing' inside Kafka, not exactly-once delivery over a network — the FLP/two-generals limit is dodged with idempotence, not defeated
Ordering is a separate axis from delivery count: you can have at-least-once and still lose ordering
Cost ladder: at-most-once cheapest, at-least-once modest, exactly-once adds coordination and latency
Rule of thumb: metrics/logs tolerate at-most-once; billing/ledgers demand exactly-once or idempotent sinks
Comparison row: at-most-once → fire-and-forget; at-least-once → ack + retry; exactly-once → ack + retry + dedup/transaction

chapters.title: Producer Path: acks, Retries, and Durability
points: acks=0: producer never waits for a broker response — at-most-once, highest throughput, silent loss on broker or network failure
acks=1: leader writes to its log and replies before followers replicate — loss if the leader dies before replication
acks=all (acks=-1): leader waits for all in-sync replicas — required for any at-least-once or exactly-once claim
min.insync.replicas: broker/topic setting for how many replicas must be in sync; acks=all with min.insync.replicas=1 still loses data
Standard durable combo: replication.factor=3, min.insync.replicas=2, acks=all — tolerates one broker loss without loss or stall
NotEnoughReplicasException is thrown when in-sync replicas drop below min.insync.replicas — the producer stalls instead of silently losing
retries defaults to Integer.MAX_VALUE in modern clients; delivery.timeout.ms (default 120000) is the real deadline
retry.backoff.ms spaces attempts; request.timeout.ms bounds a single attempt, not the whole send
Retries are exactly where duplicates come from: broker committed the batch, ack lost, producer resends
max.in.flight.requests.per.connection > 1 with retries can reorder batches (batch 2 succeeds, batch 1 retries in after)
Idempotent producer relaxes this: up to 5 in-flight requests remain safe and ordered
unclean.leader.election.enable=true lets an out-of-sync replica become leader — silently truncates committed data; keep it false
Producer callback / Future must be checked — an async send() that ignores the exception is at-most-once regardless of acks
Code: producer.send(record, (meta, ex) -> { if (ex != null) handleFailure(record, ex); })
enable.idempotence=true (default since 3.0) implies acks=all, retries>0, max.in.flight<=5 — setting a conflicting value now fails config validation

chapters.title: Idempotent Producer: PID, Sequence Numbers, Dedup
points: Goal: make a producer retry a no-op on the broker so at-least-once delivery yields exactly-once writes to a partition
Enable with enable.idempotence=true — on by default in Kafka 3.0+
Broker assigns each producer session a PID (producer ID) via an InitProducerId request
Producer stamps every record batch with (PID, epoch, base sequence number), monotonically increasing per partition
Broker keeps the last 5 sequence numbers per (PID, partition) in the producer state snapshot
Duplicate detection: incoming sequence <= last accepted → broker returns success without appending (silent dedup)
Gap detection: incoming sequence > last+1 → OutOfOrderSequenceException, meaning a batch was permanently lost
Epoch bumps fence an older zombie instance of the same producer ID
Scope limit: dedup is per (PID, partition) and per producer session — restart the process, get a new PID, lose the dedup window
Scope limit: covers only broker-side duplicates from retries; it does not dedupe your application calling send() twice
transactional.id is what makes the PID stable across restarts — without it idempotence is session-scoped
producer.id.expiration.ms (default 86400000) ages out idle producer state on the broker
Overhead: a few bytes per batch plus broker-side state; effectively free compared to transactions
Gotcha: idempotence gives no cross-partition atomicity — a send to two partitions can half-succeed
Gotcha: high partition-count producers grow broker producer-state memory; watch it on brokers with many idle PIDs

chapters.title: Consumer Path: Offsets and Commit Timing
points: An offset is a per-(topic, partition) position; the committed offset is the next record to read, not the last one read
Committed offsets live in the internal compacted topic __consumer_offsets, keyed by (group, topic, partition)
Commit-before-process = at-most-once: a crash after commit skips unprocessed records
Process-before-commit = at-least-once: a crash after processing but before commit reprocesses the batch
enable.auto.commit=true commits asynchronously every auto.commit.interval.ms (default 5000) inside poll()
Auto-commit is at-least-once, not at-most-once — the commit fires on the next poll, after the previous batch was handed out
But auto-commit becomes at-most-once if you hand records to a background thread and return from poll() immediately
commitSync() blocks and retries retriable errors; commitAsync() is fast but does not retry (a later commit supersedes it)
Standard pattern: commitAsync() in the loop, commitSync() in the finally block on shutdown
Code: try { for (rec : records) process(rec); consumer.commitAsync(); } finally { consumer.commitSync(); consumer.close(); }
Manual per-partition commit: consumer.commitSync(Map.of(tp, new OffsetAndMetadata(rec.offset() + 1))) — the +1 is mandatory
auto.offset.reset (earliest / latest / none) only applies when no valid committed offset exists — 'latest' silently skips a backlog
Rebalance re-delivers uncommitted records to the new owner — a rebalance during a slow batch is a duplicate factory
ConsumerRebalanceListener.onPartitionsRevoked is your last chance to commit before losing a partition
max.poll.interval.ms (default 300000) exceeded → the consumer is kicked out, its commit fails with CommitFailedException, and the batch is reprocessed

chapters.title: Transactions: Atomic Multi-Partition Writes
points: A transaction makes writes across multiple topic-partitions, plus offset commits, atomically visible or invisible
Solves the consume-transform-produce problem: output records and input offsets commit together or not at all
transactional.id must be set, unique per logical producer instance, and stable across restarts
Producer lifecycle: initTransactions() once, then beginTransaction() / send() … / commitTransaction() or abortTransaction()
sendOffsetsToTransaction(offsets, consumerGroupMetadata) folds the input offset commit into the same transaction
Code skeleton: producer.beginTransaction(); results.forEach(producer::send); producer.sendOffsetsToTransaction(offsets, groupMeta); producer.commitTransaction();
Any exception in the block → producer.abortTransaction() and reprocess; ProducerFencedException means exit, do not retry
The consumer feeding a transactional producer must have enable.auto.commit=false — offsets belong to the transaction
Transaction Coordinator: a broker-side component per transactional.id, chosen by hashing into the internal __transaction_state topic
Two-phase commit: coordinator writes PREPARE_COMMIT, writes control markers to every touched partition, then writes COMPLETE_COMMIT
Commit markers (control batches) are stored in the partition log itself and consume an offset, so offsets can have visible gaps
transaction.timeout.ms (default 60000) bounds an open transaction; it must be <= the broker's transaction.max.timeout.ms (default 900000)
Zombie fencing: initTransactions() bumps the epoch, and any older producer with the same transactional.id gets ProducerFencedException
Scope limit: transactions are Kafka-to-Kafka only — an external database write inside the block is not covered
Kafka Streams gets all of this with one line: processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2

chapters.title: read_committed: The Consumer Side of EOS
points: isolation.level=read_uncommitted is the default — the consumer sees transactional records the instant they are written, even if later aborted
isolation.level=read_committed makes the consumer skip aborted records and withhold uncommitted ones
Without read_committed the whole transaction machinery buys you nothing on the read side
Last Stable Offset (LSO): the offset of the earliest still-open transaction; a read_committed consumer never reads past it
So a read_committed consumer can be blocked by one long-running open transaction on that partition, even though other records are committed
The broker sends the aborted-transaction index alongside the fetch; the client filters aborted batches out
Control markers are filtered by the client and never surface as records to your application
Consequence: consecutive record offsets can be non-contiguous — never assume offset+1 is the next record
consumer.position() can exceed the last returned record's offset because of markers and filtered batches
Added latency: records become visible only at commit time, so end-to-end latency includes the transaction duration
Design implication: keep transactions short — batch size trades throughput against consumer visibility lag
A stuck transaction blocks LSO until transaction.timeout.ms forces an abort; watch the consumer-lag-with-no-progress symptom
read_committed does not deduplicate — it only hides aborted data; application-level duplicates still get through
Comparison row: read_uncommitted → lowest latency, sees dirty data; read_committed → clean data, LSO-bounded latency

chapters.title: Building the Exactly-Once Pipeline End to End
points: Exactly-once requires all four together: idempotent producer, transactional writes, read_committed consumer, and no auto-commit
Full config set: enable.idempotence=true, acks=all, transactional.id=<stable-unique>, isolation.level=read_committed, enable.auto.commit=false
Broker side: replication.factor>=3, min.insync.replicas=2, unclean.leader.election.enable=false
The read-process-write loop: poll → transform → beginTransaction → send outputs → sendOffsetsToTransaction → commit
One transactional producer per consumer instance; sharing a transactional.id across instances causes mutual fencing
Static membership (group.instance.id) reduces rebalance churn that would otherwise abort in-flight transactions
Kafka Streams exactly_once_v2 (Kafka 2.5+) uses one producer per instance instead of one per partition — far cheaper than the old exactly_once
exactly_once_v2 requires brokers 2.5+; the deprecated exactly_once and exactly_once_beta names are gone in 4.0
Streams state stores are made exactly-once by writing changelog records inside the same transaction
For a non-Kafka sink, transactions stop at the boundary — use an idempotent write or the transactional outbox pattern instead
Idempotent sink pattern: upsert by a deterministic key derived from (topic, partition, offset) or a business key
Transactional outbox pattern: write to your database and an outbox table in one DB transaction, then relay the outbox to Kafka
Two-phase commit across Kafka and a database is possible but slow and operationally fragile — prefer idempotency
Test the guarantee, don't assume it: kill brokers and consumers mid-batch and count output keys
Checklist row: any single missing setting (a stray auto-commit, a default isolation.level) silently downgrades you to at-least-once

chapters.title: Trade-offs: Throughput, Latency, Cost
points: acks=0 vs acks=all: latency rises from one network hop to leader + slowest in-sync replica round trip
Idempotence overhead is small: a sequence number per batch and broker-side state, typically low single-digit percent
Transaction overhead is per-transaction, not per-record — amortize it by batching more records per transaction
Two extra coordinator round trips plus a control marker write per partition per transaction
Confluent's measured cost: roughly 3-20% throughput hit depending on batch size; small transactions hurt most
Latency floor for read_committed consumers = transaction duration, because nothing is visible before commit
Sizing rule: 100ms commit interval is a common Streams default balancing latency against per-transaction cost
linger.ms and batch.size matter more than the EOS settings for raw throughput — batching amortizes everything
compression.type=lz4/zstd cuts network and disk cost, and is applied per batch so bigger batches compress better
Broker memory grows with the number of live PIDs and open transactions; many short-lived producers is an anti-pattern
__transaction_state and __consumer_offsets are extra write load — they are real topics with real replication
Rebalances get more expensive under EOS because open transactions must be aborted and reprocessed
Comparison row: at-most-once → highest throughput, lowest safety; at-least-once → ~95% of it with no loss; exactly-once → 80-95% with full safety
Decision guide: use at-least-once plus an idempotent sink first; reach for transactions only when the sink cannot be made idempotent

chapters.title: Failure Modes and Common Mistakes
points: Mistake: acks=all with min.insync.replicas=1 — believing you are durable while a single-replica window loses data
Mistake: unclean.leader.election.enable=true in a 'high availability' config — it trades committed data for uptime
Mistake: leaving enable.auto.commit=true inside a transactional application, committing offsets outside the transaction
Mistake: leaving isolation.level at read_uncommitted downstream and then wondering why aborted records appear
Mistake: reusing one transactional.id across parallel instances — they fence each other into a ProducerFencedException loop
Mistake: generating a random transactional.id at startup — fencing breaks and the old zombie keeps writing
Mistake: ignoring the send() callback exception, or calling future.get() nowhere — silent at-most-once
Mistake: committing offsets before processing 'to avoid duplicates' — that is choosing data loss
Mistake: slow processing exceeding max.poll.interval.ms, causing a rebalance loop and endless reprocessing; fix with max.poll.records or a worker thread with pause()
Mistake: assuming exactly-once covers side effects — the external email/HTTP call still fires twice on reprocessing
Mistake: retrying after ProducerFencedException, OutOfOrderSequenceException, or an authorization error — these are fatal, close the producer
Mistake: a long transaction stalling LSO and freezing every read_committed consumer on that partition
Mistake: assuming ordering survives — max.in.flight>1 without idempotence reorders on retry
Mistake: log retention or compaction deleting records before a lagging consumer reads them — retention loss looks like delivery loss
Debugging cue: duplicates with matching offsets = consumer-side redelivery; duplicates with different offsets = producer-side resend

chapters.title: Summary and Decision Cheat Sheet
points: At-most-once config: acks=0 or acks=1, enable.auto.commit=true with async handoff — use for metrics, traces, sampled telemetry
At-least-once config: acks=all, min.insync.replicas=2, enable.idempotence=true, manual commit after processing — the correct default for most systems
Exactly-once config: at-least-once plus transactional.id, sendOffsetsToTransaction, and isolation.level=read_committed
Idempotent producer kills producer-retry duplicates; transactions kill partial writes; read_committed kills aborted reads; each fixes a different failure
Guarantee ladder: no acks → acks=all → idempotence → transactions → read_committed consumer
Nothing Kafka offers makes a non-idempotent external side effect exactly-once — that is your application's job
Kafka Streams gives the full pipeline via processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2 and is the shortest correct path
Defaults to remember: enable.idempotence=true and acks=all since 3.0; isolation.level=read_uncommitted always
Cheapest big win: turn on idempotence and set min.insync.replicas=2 — near-zero cost, removes the most common duplicate and loss paths
Prefer an idempotent or upsert-keyed sink over transactions when you control the sink schema
Always +1 when committing an offset manually, and never assume offsets are contiguous under read_committed
Verify with chaos: kill the leader, kill the consumer mid-transaction, and assert output counts by key
Monitor: consumer lag, LSO lag, transaction abort rate, and record-error-rate on the producer
Final principle: pick the weakest guarantee your correctness requirements allow, then make it airtight rather than reaching for exactly-once by reflex
